# Work with me

A sensible first step is a paid diagnostic with a clear question and a clear deliverable. Everything else builds from there.

## Ways to engage
- **Diagnostic.** Evidence, priorities, and a recommended next step, for a defined site and a defined set of questions. Usually one to three weeks.
- **Implementation sprint.** Agreed fixes or deliverables, verified on the live site against written acceptance criteria.
- **Migration review.** Pre-launch or post-launch checks and developer coordination for a named site and launch.
- **Ongoing support.** An agreed monthly capacity for SEO, content, and website work.
- **Advisory.** A monthly advisory retainer, or individual briefings, workshops, and second opinions.
- **AI pilot.** One useful workflow built and demonstrated, with defined inputs, permissions, outputs, and handover.

## How a project runs
1. **First conversation.** You describe the site and the problem by email or in a short call. I say whether I'm the right person and where I'd start.
2. **Scope in writing.** The questions, the deliverable, the access needed, the timeline, and the price, agreed before work begins.
3. **Payment.** The diagnostic is prepaid; larger projects start with a deposit.
4. **The work.** I investigate, report progress in writing, and raise anything urgent at once.
5. **Delivery.** Findings, fixes, tickets, or the agreed deliverable, walked through with you and your team.
6. **Verification.** A check of the live result once changes ship, and a recommendation for what comes next.

## Payment terms
- Diagnostics, briefings, and second opinions are prepaid.
- Projects start with a deposit.
- Retainers are billed at the start of each month.
- Invoices are due on receipt, and work continues once they're paid.

## Where the work happens

Every project runs in Basecamp or by email, threaded and on the record, so you always know the status and nothing gets lost. Developer work goes into your ticket system.

## What helps
- Access to Search Console, analytics, and the CMS, repository, or DNS I'll work in.
- An introduction to your developer, host, or marketing team.
- Prompt answers. A project that goes quiet closes, and restarts with a fresh scope when you're ready.

## Hosting

I work on sites wherever they're hosted. Hosting itself stays with you or your provider, so you always own and control your site.

## Upwork

If your company hires through Upwork, you can hire me there: [Chris Abraham on Upwork](https://www.upwork.com/freelancers/chrisjabraham).

More answers on the [FAQ](https://gerriscorp.com/faq/).

[Start with a diagnostic](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/)

# Frequently asked questions

Practical answers about process, timing, payment, and how I work.

## Starting out

### How does a project start?

With an email or a short call about your site and the problem. If I'm the right person, I send a written scope for a paid diagnostic: the questions, the deliverable, the access needed, the timeline, and the price.

### Do you offer a free audit?

The first conversation is free and short, enough to tell whether I can help and where I'd start. The diagnosis itself is paid work, because that's where the real value is.

### Who does the work?

I do, personally, on every engagement. Gerris Corp is my consultancy.

### What kinds of clients do you work with?

Funded companies, established businesses, agencies that need a specialist, and individuals whose public record matters, in any industry and any country.

## Timing

### How long does a diagnostic take?

Usually one to three weeks, depending on the size of the site and the number of separate problems. The timeline is agreed in writing before work starts.

### How soon can you start?

Usually within one to two weeks of a signed scope and payment. Urgent problems, such as a sudden traffic collapse or a failed launch, get priority when I have capacity.

### How long until results show in Google?

Fixes take effect as Google recrawls the affected pages: days for important pages, weeks or months for large sites. I track the change in Search Console and report it.

## Payment

### How do you charge?

Diagnostics, briefings, and second opinions are prepaid at a fixed price. Larger projects start with a deposit. Ongoing support and advisory retainers are billed monthly in advance.

### Can I hire you through Upwork?

Yes. Many clients hire me through Upwork, which handles contracts and payment.

## Working together

### What access do you need?

Usually Search Console, analytics, and read access to the CMS or repository. DNS and CDN access when the work involves them. I document every account I use.

### Which platforms do you work on?

WordPress, Umbraco, Wix, Squarespace, Shopify, Magento, Netlify, GitHub Pages, static sites, and JavaScript frameworks such as Next.js, React, Vue, and Alpine.js, with Cloudflare in front of many of them.

### How do you communicate during a project?

In writing, in Basecamp or by email, so every decision and status update is on the record. Calls are scheduled when they're useful.

### Do you work with in-house developers?

Yes, and it's one of the things I do best. I write precise tickets with acceptance criteria and check the result once it ships.

### Is the work confidential?

Yes. I name clients only with their permission, and I'm happy to sign a nondisclosure agreement.

Something else? [Ask me directly](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/).

# Editorial standards

Gerris Corp is one consultant, so every guide, case study, and service page on this site is mine to stand behind. These are the rules I hold them to.

## Experience comes first

A case study here exists because I did the work: I was hired, I ran the diagnosis or the build, and I can say exactly which parts were mine and which belonged to the client's developer or agency. Guides grow out of the same engagements. If I haven't done something with my own hands, I don't write a how-to about it.

## Claims point to their source

When a guide says how Googlebot renders a page, how Bing treats a tag, what an RFC requires of a DNS record, or what a consent setting actually does, the page lists the documentation behind it under "References." The same list is published in the guide's structured data. Official documentation changes, so a reference is a starting point for your own check, not a replacement for it.

## AI in the workflow, with a human at the end

I build with AI tools every day, including Claude Code, and this site's generator and many first drafts came out of that work. The rule is simple: nothing goes live until I've read it, corrected it, and verified every factual statement. Biographical details about me come from my own records and published sources I can point to, never from what a chatbot has decided about me. The build itself refuses pages that break the house rules for titles, length, duplication, and voice.

## Confidentiality is part of accuracy

Clients are described by industry and problem. No names, addresses, revenue, case numbers, or private screenshots, and nothing that would let a reader work out who the client is. Ongoing and paused engagements are labeled that way. Outcomes are reported only when the evidence supports them, and "under way" is an honest status.

## No one pays to be mentioned

This site carries no affiliate links, sponsored content, or paid reviews. When I name a tool, a host, or a platform, it's because I use it or a client runs on it.

## Dates mean something

Every page shows its last update, and guides show both their publication and revision dates. When Google, Bing, or a standard changes in a way that affects a guide, the guide is revised and the date moves.

## Found a mistake?

Email [chris@gerriscorp.com](mailto:chris@gerriscorp.com) with the page address and the problem. I'll check it against the source and correct the page if you're right, and note any substantive change on the page itself.

## More about me

My background is on the [About page](https://gerriscorp.com/about/), how engagements run is on [Work With Me](https://gerriscorp.com/work-with-me/), and you can reach me through the [contact page](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/).

# Colophon

A colophon is the note at the back of a well-made book about how it was made. This is that note for gerriscorp.com.

## The logo

The Gerris water strider was designed and drawn in 2012 by [Oliver Uberti](https://www.oliveruberti.com/), a dear friend and a remarkable artist. Oliver was a senior design editor at National Geographic and is the co-author and designer of Atlas of the Invisible, London: The Information Capital, Where the Animals Go, and Notes from a Public Typewriter. He gave the company its emblem: *Gerris lacustris*, the insect that skates across the surface of a pond without breaking it.

The name came first, and it came from rowing. Carbon fiber racing shells, especially doubles, have always looked to me like the pond skaters you can find in the still water along the Potomac's banks, dancing on the surface tension. I named my Hudson racing shell *Gerris* before I ever named a company after it. Once the firm Dan Krueger and I ran was incorporated, I asked Oliver for a logo, and what he drew settled the matter: any thought of renaming the agency ended the day I saw it. I wrote the whole story up in 2017.

## Design

The look borrows from the classic Plone theme I've used for my own sites for two decades: tabbed navigation, slate blue links, and nothing between the reader and the words. Body text is black Verdana at 18 pixels for legibility. The accent colors, a burnt orange for the name, a blue for page titles, and a teal for section heads, were each darkened until they pass the WCAG contrast standard against white.

## How it's built

Every page starts as a plain HTML file. A small Python program reads them, wraps each in the shared header and footer, and writes the finished site: pages, a Markdown copy of each page for AI tools, XML and HTML sitemaps, an Atom feed, llms.txt, and redirect pages for more than 400 addresses from the old gerriscorp.com. Before anything is published, the same program checks every page: title and description lengths, one heading per page, minimum word counts, first person singular, no copied phrasing between pages, and no broken internal links. If a page fails, nothing ships.

The site was written and built in a terminal, over SSH from a ThinkPad X220 to a Linux server at DigitalOcean, working alongside Claude Code, Anthropic's AI coding assistant. I set the requirements, made the editorial calls, and checked every fact; the assistant wrote code and drafts to my direction. [The editorial standards](https://gerriscorp.com/standards/) describe how that division of labor works.

## Hosting and delivery

The finished files are served by GitHub Pages over HTTPS, with DNS at Cloudflare. There's no database, no content management system, and no server code to patch. The only script is Google Analytics, set up with consent mode, as described on the [privacy page](https://gerriscorp.com/privacy/).

## Tested with
- Lynx, the text browser, to see each page the way screen readers and crawlers receive it. My notes on that are in [Lynx for website QA](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/lynx-qa/).
- Google PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse, for performance, accessibility, best practices, and SEO.
- Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, with IndexNow announcing every change to Bing.

## Source

The code and content live in a public repository: [github.com/chrisabraham/gerriscorp](https://github.com/chrisabraham/gerriscorp). The site went live on October 5, 2026.

# Privacy

This site collects very little: anonymous visit statistics, and whatever you choose to send me by email or phone.

## Visit statistics

This site uses Google Analytics 4 to count visits, see which pages people read, and learn how visitors arrive, including from search engines and AI assistants. It records information such as the pages you view, your approximate location, your device and browser, and the site that referred you. It doesn't collect your name, email address, or other details that identify you directly.

For visitors in the United Kingdom and the European Economic Area, analytics cookies are switched off. Google Analytics receives cookieless measurements instead, which count visits without storing anything on your device. Elsewhere, Google Analytics may set first-party cookies to recognize repeat visits. Advertising and personalization features are turned off for everyone.

Google processes this data under its own [privacy policy](https://policies.google.com/privacy). You can block Google Analytics anywhere with your browser's privacy settings, a content blocker, or Google's [opt-out browser add-on](https://tools.google.com/dlpage/gaoptout).

## Email and phone

When you email me or call, I receive what you send: your name, your address or number, and the details of your project. I use it only to reply and to do the work you hire me for. I don't sell it, share it with marketers, or add you to a mailing list.

## Hosting and security

The site is static pages served by GitHub Pages, with DNS through Cloudflare. Those services keep standard server logs, such as IP addresses and request times, for security and reliability, under their own policies. There are no forms, accounts, or comments on this site.

## Client information

Information I see while working for clients, such as analytics, Search Console data, site access, and documents, is kept confidential, used only for the engagement, and covered by a nondisclosure agreement where the client asks for one.

## Questions

Email [chris@gerriscorp.com](mailto:chris@gerriscorp.com) with any question about your information, or to ask me to delete correspondence you've sent.

- [Core Web Vitals explained: LCP, INP, CLS, and the fixes that work](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/core-web-vitals/): What Google measures with Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint, and Cumulative Layout Shift, how to read field data, and the fixes for each one.
- [Cloudflare settings that help or hurt SEO and AI crawlers](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/cloudflare-seo/): The Cloudflare settings that decide whether Googlebot, Bingbot, and AI crawlers can reach your site, plus the caching, HTTPS, and redirect choices that help.

- [sitemap.xml](https://gerriscorp.com/sitemap.xml): the XML sitemap for search engines.
